813.title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
813.hook: "I will take away the stony heart... and I will give you a heart of flesh"
813.carry: flesh is more vulnerable than stone
813.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the promise of a new heart and a new spirit is often studied alongside Jeremiah's covenant written on the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezekiel's charge against the shepherds who fed themselves, and God's promise to seek the lost and bind up the broken. Today, a promise about the heart.

A stone in your pocket stays the same temperature as whatever is around it. Cold on a cold day, warm in the sun. It doesn't bruise or bleed. It also doesn't feel, and it can't grow. Sometimes a heart starts to work like that: after a loss, after a betrayal, after one too many disappointments. It's protection. It's also a kind of stone. Ezekiel, speaking to exiles who have lost their land, their Temple and their king, uses exactly that picture, and then makes a promise about it.
screen: `A STONE DOESN'T BRUISE.` → `IT ALSO DOESN'T FEEL.` → `A PROMISE ABOUT HEARTS.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." The Hebrew word here is lev, heart, and some readers point out that in the Bible the heart thinks and chooses, not only feels. Read that way, a heart of stone isn't just a cold heart. It's a mind that can't take anything new in, a will that won't move. And a heart of flesh isn't a weak heart. It's a living one: it can be pressed, it can respond, it can be written on. That connects back to Jeremiah's covenant, written on the heart. You can't write on stone without a chisel. You can write on flesh with a touch. Notice who does the work. Earlier in the book, Ezekiel tells the people to make themselves a new heart. Here it's the other way: I will give, I will take away, I will put within you. Some readers hold the two together: a person turns, and is also helped to turn. The verse right after says the new spirit will help the people walk in God's ways. And it's spoken to a whole people; in Hebrew the you is plural. It's a promise to a community gone hard: you will feel again. Flesh is more vulnerable than stone. That's the gift.

segments.voice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, and ask gently: where have I gone a little bit stone, toward a person, a place, a part of my past, a kind of news I've stopped letting in? Don't force it open; just notice it, and breathe toward it, the way you'd warm cold hands. If you pray, you can say the verse as a prayer: a new heart also will I give you.
lev, the Hebrew word for heart, which in the Bible thinks and chooses, not only feels, and which Ezekiel promises God will change from stone into flesh. Today's word.
Your line: flesh is more vulnerable than stone. A living heart can still be written on. See you tomorrow.

814.title: Can these bones live? (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
814.hook: the valley of dry bones, read on the Shabbat of Passover
814.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 37:1–14 as the prophetic reading on the Shabbat during Passover, and Jewish prayer speaks of God who gives life to the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise of a heart of flesh: flesh is more vulnerable than stone. Today, something far harder than stone.

The hand of the Lord takes hold of Ezekiel and sets him down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones. He's led around them, round about, the text says, and he sees there are very many, and they are very dry. Not a fresh battlefield: bones bleached and scattered, long past anyone's grief. And then comes the question, put to the prophet as he stands there: "Son of man, can these bones live?"
screen: `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, VERY DRY.` → `CAN THESE BONES LIVE?`

segments.voice: Ezekiel's answer is short and honest: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." Not yes, not no. He hands the question back. Then he's told to speak to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD." As he speaks, there is a noise, a shaking, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin covers them. And the text stops on a chilling detail: there was no breath in them. So he's told to speak a second time, to the wind, the breath. The chapter keeps returning to one Hebrew word, ruach, and the King James renders it breath, wind and spirit. Come from the four winds, O breath. The breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, a great army. Then the chapter says what the vision means. These bones are the whole house of Israel, saying: "Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost." And the answer: I will open your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel, and put my spirit in you, and you shall live. Some readers hear in it the return of an exiled people to their land. Others hear a promise of the resurrection of the dead, a belief Jewish prayer holds. The rabbis of the Talmud even argued about whether it really happened or was a parable. And Jews read this chapter in synagogue on the Shabbat that falls during Passover, the festival of a people brought out alive.

segments.voice: Sit still first, like the bones before the breath came, and let four breaths arrive on their own: ruach, the word the chapter keeps using. Then bring to mind one thing you've written off, a skill your hands used to know, a song you stopped singing, and ask honestly: can this live? You don't have to answer; you can say what Ezekiel said, thou knowest, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ruach. Hebrew for breath, wind, spirit: the question put to Ezekiel in a valley of dry bones, before it comes into them and they stand. Today's word.
Your line: bone to its bone. The breath came after the bones were joined. Day eight hundred fourteen, done.

815.title: Two sticks (Ezekiel 37:15–28)
815.hook: the sticks of Judah and Joseph become one in the prophet's hand
815.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 37:15–28 as the prophetic reading for the Torah portion Vayigash, where Joseph and Judah meet, and the hope of gathering the scattered appears in daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a valley of dry bones, breath from the four winds, and they stood: bone to its bone. Today, the same chapter goes on, with two pieces of wood.

Two sticks. That's all Ezekiel needs for today's message. No vision this time, no fire, no wheels. He's told to write a name on each one. On the first: For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions. On the second: For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions. Two names that stood for the two kingdoms, south and north, and the north had been carried off and scattered. And then he's told to hold them.
screen: `TWO PIECES OF WOOD.` → `ONE FOR JUDAH, ONE FOR JOSEPH.` → `HOLD THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction, in the King James words: "And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand." From where the people stand: two sticks, end to end, held in one fist, the prophet's hand closed around the seam. It's street theater, meant to make people ask. So the text gives them their question: wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest by these? And the answer: God will take the stick of Joseph and join it with the stick of Judah, and they shall be one in mine hand. Notice the shift. First, one in thy hand, the prophet's. Then, one in mine hand, God's. In the text, the prophet's small act pictures something God says he will finish. Then the promise is spelled out. The scattered will be gathered from among the nations and brought home. They shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all. One king. One people. A covenant of peace, and God's dwelling place with them. Remember the north falling, a few weeks back, its people carried off to Assyria. Here a prophet says the story isn't over. Jewish tradition carries the hope of gathering the scattered in its prayers. And the image also works at kitchen-table size: two people who stopped speaking, two halves of a family, two parts of yourself that don't get along. The prophet doesn't glue the sticks. He holds them together in his hand, and waits for the rest.

segments.voice: If there are two pens or spoons nearby, pick them up; if not, just open your hands, and bring to mind two things split apart: two people, two sides of a family, two parts of your own life. Let one rest in each hand, then slowly bring your hands together and hold them as one, without solving anything. If you pray, you can place them in God's hand.
Two sticks. Ezekiel writes Judah on one and Joseph on the other, and holds them so they become one in his hand: a promise that the divided will be joined. Today's word.
Your line: one in thy hand. Then, one in God's hand, as the text promises. Until tomorrow.

816.title: The river from the Temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12)
816.hook: a river deepens and heals the salt sea; everything lives where it goes
816.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 47 within the book's closing vision of a rebuilt Temple (chapters 40–48), and the Talmud remembers Hananiah ben Hezekiah working through those chapters to reconcile their laws with the Torah's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two sticks, Judah and Joseph, joined into one in the prophet's hand. Today, the last of our days in Ezekiel.

Ankles. Knees. Waist. Then water to swim in. Near the end of his book, Ezekiel is shown a vision of the Temple rebuilt, and his guide brings him back to the door of the house. There's water seeping out from under the threshold, flowing east. A trickle. The guide walks out with a measuring line, measures a distance, and leads Ezekiel through: the water is to his ankles. Another measure: to his knees. Another: to his loins. Another, and it's a river he can't cross, waters to swim in.
screen: `WATER UNDER THE THRESHOLD.` → `ANKLES, KNEES, WAIST.` → `A RIVER TOO DEEP TO CROSS.`

segments.voice: Water that seeps out under a door usually spreads out and soaks away. This water does the opposite. With no stream feeding it that the text mentions, it keeps getting deeper. Then the guide asks Ezekiel a question: son of man, hast thou seen this? He's brought back along the bank, and now he sees very many trees on both sides. The river flows down into the desert and into the sea, and the waters are healed. Here's the line the whole chapter turns on, in the King James words: "every thing shall live whither the river cometh." Fishermen will stand on the shore and spread their nets, and the fish will be many. The trees along the banks will bear fruit every month, and their leaves won't wither. And the last detail: "the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine." Food and healing, from water that started under a door. Ezekiel's book began with exiles sitting by a foreign river, the Chebar, far from the Temple. Near its end, a river flows out from the Temple, so deep it can't be crossed, bringing life even to the sea. Some readers hear it as God's presence flowing out from the house. And notice where it starts: not as a river at all, but as a seep under a door, measured again and again as it goes.

segments.voice: Find something in your life that's still at the ankles: a practice you just started, a new friendship, something you're learning, maybe even this daily habit. Without pushing, picture walking a little farther in, ankles, then knees, and let the breath be the measuring line, one length at a time. If you pray, you can ask that it bring life where it goes.
Chebar, the foreign river where Ezekiel's exiles once sat, far from the Temple whose own river later heals the sea. Today's word.

817.title: Twelve small books
817.hook: twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll
817.howItsDone: In Jewish Bibles the twelve short prophets, Hosea through Malachi, are grouped as one book called Trei Asar, and passages from them are read as haftarot in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river ran out from under the Temple door in Ezekiel's vision, recalling the Chebar where the exiles once sat, rising as it went, until the salt sea was healed. Your line was everything lives where it flows. Today, Ezekiel's book closes, and a crowded scroll opens.

How do you keep a small book from getting lost? Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel each fill a long book of their own. After them come twelve more prophets, and some of their books are short enough to read on a bus ride. A herdsman from Tekoa. A man who ran from God by ship. A prophet who spoke against one neighboring nation, Edom. Instead of twelve little scrolls, tradition wrote them end to end, on one.
screen: `ONE SCROLL, TWELVE NAMES.` → `SHORT ENOUGH FOR A BUS RIDE.` → `WRITTEN END TO END.`

segments.voice: Trei Asar. It's Aramaic, and it simply means twelve. Not the minor prophets. Just: the Twelve. Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Said out loud, it sounds like a class roll call. So why one scroll? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, asks about the order of the prophets. Near the start of Hosea's book come the words, the beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea, and the rabbis take that to mean his prophecy came early. Then why isn't his book placed before Isaiah? Their answer is plain. Hosea is written together with the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, and because his book is small, it might get lost. A short scroll can slip behind a shelf. Twelve, sewn into one, stay found: a kind of protection for the quiet ones. And they're quiet only on the outside. Inside: a prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel. A prophet who asks for justice to well up as waters. A runaway swallowed by a great fish. Lines still read aloud in synagogue. In the Talmud's list of the prophets, the Twelve appear under that one name, as a single book. That's how a small voice lasts: not alone, but bound in with others. Over the next stretch of days, this path walks through the scroll, one prophet at a time.

segments.voice: If there's a Bible or a reading app nearby, open to any of the Twelve and read one short chapter slowly, start to finish, with no study notes, just the words. If you'd rather not read right now, say the twelve names once, slowly, and let one of them stay with you. If you pray, you can ask to hear one small voice clearly.
Trei Asar. Aramaic for twelve: the twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll so none of them would be lost. Today's word.
Your line: small books, big voices. Twelve prophets, one scroll, none of them lost. Day eight hundred seventeen.

818.title: Hosea: betrothed again (Hosea 2:16–22)
818.hook: a broken marriage restored becomes a picture of God and Israel
818.howItsDone: Jews who wear tefillin often recite Hosea 2:21–22 on weekday mornings while winding the tefillin strap around the middle finger, and the verses are part of the haftarah for the Torah portion Bamidbar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trei Asar: twelve short prophets bound on one scroll so none of them would get lost. Your line was small books, big voices. Today, the first voice on that scroll.

The first thing Hosea is asked to do is marry. He marries Gomer, and the marriage goes wrong. In the chapters that follow, the book speaks of a wife who goes after other lovers, and it doesn't look away from the hurt. Children with names that sound like verdicts. Anger, accusation, a house gone cold. A story could end there. This one doesn't. Somewhere in the middle of the second chapter, the voice changes, and a door opens in the wall.
screen: `A PROPHET IS TOLD TO MARRY.` → `THE MARRIAGE BREAKS.` → `THEN THE VOICE CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Hosea's marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel: a covenant like a wedding, a people who wandered after other gods, a love that's been wounded. And in chapter two, God speaks like a husband who wants to begin again. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "I will allure her, And bring her into the wilderness, And speak tenderly unto her." The wilderness, not as punishment, but as the place where the first love began, after Egypt, before all the trouble. The valley of Achor, remembered for an old trouble, becomes, the text says, "a door of hope." Then a small, sharp change of names. On that day, the text says, you will call me Ishi, my husband, and no more Baali. Baali can also mean my husband, but it echoes the god Baal, and the next verse says the names of the Baalim will be taken out of her mouth. The bond is to be personal again, not one more lord among lords. Then the vows, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever; Yea, I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, And in lovingkindness, and in compassion. And I will betroth thee unto Me in faithfulness." Betroth, three times. Not remarried: betrothed, as if engaged for the first time. And the gifts aren't jewelry. They're righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion, faithfulness. Some Jews say these lines each weekday morning, while winding the tefillin strap around the finger, like a ring.
screen: `A MARRIAGE AS A PICTURE OF COVENANT.` · `BACK TO THE WILDERNESS, SPOKEN TO GENTLY.` · then, large: `I WILL BETROTH THEE UNTO ME FOR EVER.` · then: `SAID WHILE WINDING THE TEFILLIN STRAP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted from or grown used to, a partner, a parent, a friend, a sibling, and go back in your mind to the wilderness, to the beginning, when it was new: what did you first notice and like about them? Then ask which word from Hosea's list this bond needs most: justice, kindness, compassion or faithfulness. If you pray, you can say the betrothal line slowly.
Hosea. The prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel, and who hears God promise to betroth the people again. Today's word.
Your line: betrothed again. Back to the beginning, as if for the first time. See you tomorrow.

819.title: Hosea: take with you words (Hosea 14:2–3)
819.hook: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD"
819.howItsDone: Jews read Hosea 14 as the haftarah on Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and teshuvah, returning, is the theme of that season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea heard God promise to betroth the people again, in righteousness, justice, lovingkindness and compassion. Your line was betrothed again. Today, Hosea's last chapter, and what to bring when you come back.

"Take with you words, And return unto the LORD." That's the instruction, in the 1917 Jewish translation. Not a lamb. Not gold, or a long list of promises. Words. Hosea has spent its chapters on betrayal and hurt, on a people who kept turning away. Now, at the very end, the way home opens, and the one thing they're told to carry costs nothing and can be the hardest to find: the right words.
screen: `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` → `NOT A LAMB, NOT GOLD.` → `THE HARDEST THING TO FIND.`

segments.voice: The passage opens with one Hebrew word: shuvah. Return. "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Jewish tradition hears in it teshuvah, the word for repentance, which means turning back, coming home. And Hosea doesn't leave the words up to them. He gives them a script: say unto Him, forgive all iniquity, accept that which is good. Then a striking line. The King James has: "so will we render the calves of our lips." The 1917 Jewish translation spells out the picture: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Bulls were once brought as offerings; here the lips take their place, and words become the offering. Some readers hear a quiet idea that the rabbis made central after the Temple was gone: with no altar, prayer stands where the sacrifice stood. A sorry, said out loud, becomes a kind of gift. And notice the order. Not a feeling first. Words first. Turning back often begins with a sentence that's hard to say, and saying it changes something. Hosea knew how hard; that's why he hands them the words. The chapter gives its name to a Shabbat: Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath of Return, between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when Jews read this very passage in synagogue, at the season of turning back.
screen: `SHUVAH: RETURN.` · `HOSEA HANDS THEM THE WORDS.` · then, large: `THE CALVES OF OUR LIPS.` · then: `SHABBAT SHUVAH, THE SABBATH OF RETURN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one sorry you owe, big or small, a sharp tone, a missed call, a promise that slid, and do what Hosea does: write the script in the plainest words you can, no explanation, no defense, something like I was wrong about this, and I'm sorry. Say it silently a few times, until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can bring the same plain words to God.
Hosea. The prophet who ends his book with a way home, and tells the people to take words with them when they return. Today's word.
Your line: take with you words. The week ran from flesh is more vulnerable than stone, through dry bones and a healing river, to Hosea's way home. That's day eight hundred nineteen.
